title: Gantry Gorge

pages.text:
*The Surveyor's Catechism, Twenty-Second Saying: A bridge is a promise made out of triangles.*

The gap was three hundred feet of sheer grey rock, and it had the audacity to be in the way.

Isla stood on the lip of Gantry Gorge, her boots planted firmly on the loose scree, and looked down. The Wend river churned far below, a dark, muscular thing that had wandered from its bed twice that week and left no trace of where it had been. It was the final unclosed leg of the traverse, the last stubborn thread keeping the whole survey from snapping shut. If they could not cross, the numbers would not balance. The closing error would remain, and the Unmade would stay loose, drifting like a ship without a rudder.

"Three hundred feet," Joss said, standing beside her. He did not look down. He was looking at the far bank, his pale freckled face tight with concentration, a carpenter’s pencil tucked behind his ear. "Maybe three hundred and fifty. The fog plays with your eyes."

"Then we measure," Isla said.

She unrolled the steel tape, and Mags, with the grace of a gymnast who had never been asked to do anything graceful, anchored the zero mark on a flat outcrop. Joss crossed the gorge on a precarious rope swing, his boots skidding on the wet stone, until he reached the opposite rim. He held the tape taut, his face a mask of professional annoyance at the wind, and called out the figure.

"Four hundred and fifty links," he shouted, his voice thin in the cold air. "Allowing for sag and the temperature of this wretched morning."

Isla wrote it down. She checked the chronometer. She checked the angle of the sun. Then she took out a stub of charcoal and the back of a discarded map of the Western Marches, and began to sketch. Her hand moved with the steady, rhythmic certainty that had saved the survey more times than she could count. She drew the two abutments, the span, and then, with a quick, decisive stroke, the triangles.

"A timber truss," she said, holding the paper up to the light. "We build the falsework in the river, raise the truss from both banks, and lock the center. No arch. Arch thrust will push the abutments apart and drop us into the water."

Joss grinned, a wide, lopsided expression that crinkled the corners of his eyes. "Triangles," he said. "Yes. Strong shapes. I can do strong shapes."
pages.image: Isla in a mustard-yellow coat and dark-green trousers stands on a rocky cliff edge, holding up a piece of paper with a charcoal sketch of triangles, while Joss in a rust-red shirt and brown apron watches from across a deep, misty gorge.

pages.text:
The villagers of Ennis Vale did not ask questions. They simply appeared, moving with the steady, relentless pressure of a rising tide, bringing carts, axes, and a quiet, collective determination that seemed to vibrate in the cold air. They had waited forty-four years for something to happen, and they were not about to let a river stop it.

Joss took charge of the timber. He stood on a boulder in the shallows, shouting directions with the enthusiasm of a man who had been waiting for an excuse to break something. "Oak, not pine! Pine splinters under load. We need compression members that can take the burden of a wagon, a horse, and a very angry mule!"

Mags organized the supply line. She tied a rope to a post, then to a cart, then to her own pack, creating a pulley system of such elegant simplicity that Isla felt a pang of professional jealousy. Beams the size of tree trunks slid down the slope, rolling in the mud, and were caught by hands that looked like they had been made of rope.

Perrin Ashdown, tiny and wiry in his patched green coat, climbed the boulder where Joss stood. He held a rope end with both hands, his knuckles white, his face set in a grim line of determination.

"I am holding," he announced, his voice thin but steady. "I will hold until the end."

"You are seventy-eight years old," Joss said, not unkindly.

"And you are a fool if you think I am letting you do all the work," Perrin replied. He tightened his grip. "I held the chain when the bridge fell in '42. I can hold a rope."

Isla watched him, and felt a strange, warm pressure behind her eyes. This was what precision was for. Not just to fix the land, but to let people stand on it. To let them hold on. She picked up her level, set it on the tripod, and began to take readings for the falsework, her voice calm and measured as she called out the numbers to Mags, who scribbled them in the field-book with a speed that bordered on manic.

The sun was setting, painting the water in shades of copper and blood. The truss was half-built, a skeletal bird crouching over the river, waiting for its wings.
pages.image: Joss in a rust-red shirt and brown apron stands on a boulder shouting instructions, while tiny, white-whiskered Perrin in a patched green coat grips a thick rope with both hands, his face set in determination, as villagers haul timber up a muddy slope.

pages.text:
The rain arrived from the high fells not as drops but as a grey, silent sheet, turning the world into a blur of water and stone. It did not fall; it hung, a cold, misty curtain that soaked through their coats and into their bones. The river, which had been a churning brown ribbon, began to swell, its edges creeping up the banks, swallowing the stones where they had been working that morning.

Isla stood in the rain, her sightglass fogged, her hair plastered to her face. She held the staff, a long wooden pole with painted markings, and took readings. The water was rising. Not quickly, not dramatically, but with a steady, inexorable logic that was more terrifying than any sudden flood.

"Four feet," she called out, her voice thin in the wind.

Mags, huddled under a tarpaulin, wrote it down. "Time?"

"Ten past six."

"Five feet," Isla said, an hour later. Her hands were shaking, not from the cold, but from the effort of keeping her eye steady on the bubble in the level. The number was climbing. The falsework, the wooden scaffolding they had built in the river to support the truss, was now submerged to the topmost plank. If the water rose another foot, it would push against the timber, and the truss, still incomplete, would tilt and snap.

"We have to clear the falsework," Joss shouted over the roar of the water. He was on the far bank, his boots slipping on the wet stone. "We can’t fight the river! We have to let it pass through!"

"Then we lose the truss," Isla said. Her voice was flat, devoid of hope. "If we remove the support, the center drops."

"No," Joss said. "We don't remove it. We lighten it. We take the load off the center members first. We let the river push the falsework out of the way before it breaks it."

It was a mad idea. It was also, Isla realized, the only idea that respected the physics of the situation. The river was a force that could not be stopped, only directed. They had to yield, or break.
pages.image: Isla in a mustard-yellow coat stands in heavy rain, holding a wooden staff, her face grim and focused, while the river below swells and churns violently against the wooden scaffolding of the bridge falsework.

pages.text:
The night was cold and sharp, the rain replaced by a biting wind that cut through their cloaks. The river was high, a black, muscular torrent that roared in the dark, a constant, threatening presence that seemed to be pressing against the very stones of the gorge. The falsework was gone, swept away in a rush of splintered wood and foam, but the truss remained, a skeletal framework of oak and pine, half-finished, hanging over the abyss.

The last member, the keystone equivalent, the central tie that would lock the two halves of the truss together, was waiting on the bank. It was a massive beam, twenty feet long, heavy as a cannonball. Joss and the miller’s sons, two broad-shouldered men with faces like hammers, set up the block and tackle. They hauled the beam into position, inch by inch, their muscles straining, their breath coming in white puffs in the cold air.

Isla and Mags stood on the bank, calling out the river height. Every ten minutes, Isla took a reading. The number was climbing, but slowly. The water was at eight feet. Nine feet. Ten feet. The truss was at its highest point, the center just above the water, a fragile line of wood against the black chasm.

"It’s slipping," Joss shouted. He was on the truss, his boots on the wet timber, his face pale with exertion. "The tackle is slipping! We need more hands!"

Perrin was there. He was holding the rope, his arms trembling, his face a mask of pain and determination. He was seventy-eight years old, and he was holding the tension of the line with his bare hands. Isla watched him, and felt a surge of pride so intense it made her dizzy. This was what they were for. Not just the numbers, not just the maps, but the hands that held the line.

The beam dropped. It was not a gentle settling; it was a sudden, heavy thud, a deep, wooden knock that vibrated through the rock, through the water, through the bones of everyone who was there. The truss was locked. The bridge was whole.
pages.image: Joss in a rust-red shirt and brown apron strains on a rope on a wooden truss bridge, while tiny, white-whiskered Perrin in a patched green coat holds a thick rope with both hands, his face grim, as a massive timber beam drops into place over a dark, roaring river.

pages.text:
Dawn broke over the gorge in a wash of pale gold, the mist burning off the water in thin, curling ribbons. The bridge stood, a taut line of timber against the grey sky. The river roared beneath it, a wild, untamed thing that had been checked. Not by force. But by the careful, patient work of hands that had measured twice and built once.

Joss insisted on a load test.

It was a tradition, he said, a bridge-wright’s superstition, but a necessary one. He loaded a wagon with stones, heavy, dense, unyielding stones, and walked it across. The wagon groaned. The wheels crunched on the timber. The horses whinnied in protest. Ledger, the mule, was blindfolded and furious. He stamped his hooves, refusing to look at the water below.

Joss walked the wagon across at a crawl. His hands were on the reins. His face was set in a grim line of concentration. Isla watched the truss, her eyes tracing the triangles, the tension members, the compression chords. She listened for the creak. The snap. The groan of stressed wood. There was nothing. The bridge did not even creak. It held, steady and sure. A promise made out of triangles. A line that had been held true.

When the wagon reached the far bank, Joss turned and looked at her. His face was flushed, not from the cold, but from the effort. From the pride of a job well done. Isla crossed the bridge. Her boots were silent on the timber. She kissed him on the cheek. It was quick. Light. A small, honest gesture that said more than any words could.

Joss turned the color of a beet. His freckles disappeared under a flush of deep red. He looked at the bridge. Then at her. Then at the river. And said, very quietly, "It holds."

"Yes," Isla said. "It holds."
